name: HCG and clomiphene for voice
lead: In looksmaxxing discussion, human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) and clomiphene (clomifene) are two prescription drugs sometimes mentioned as ways of raising the body's own testosterone, with the idea that higher testosterone could support a deeper, more masculine voice and a more masculine overall presentation. Both are used medically for fertility and, off-label, for male hypogonadism.[1][2]

hCG is a hormone that resembles luteinizing hormone and stimulates the Leydig cells of the testes to make testosterone.[2] Clomiphene is a selective estrogen receptor modulator that blocks estrogen feedback in the hypothalamus, increasing GnRH, FSH and LH release.[1] Its enclomifene isomer works in a similar way and has been studied in secondary hypogonadism.[3] Encyclopedic sources on these drugs describe fertility and testosterone uses and do not describe an effect on adult voice pitch.[1][2][3]

No clinical studies of either drug for voice were found. Voice deepening is a pubertal effect of testosterone on the larynx, and voice problems that persist after puberty, such as puberphonia, are typically treated with voice therapy; hypogonadism is described as something to rule out in some cases.[4]

chain: hCG or clomiphene stimulates the body's own testosterone production

angle.text: Proponents in appearance communities reason that raising natural testosterone, without taking testosterone itself, could support a deeper voice and other masculine traits. The drugs' documented uses are fertility and treating low testosterone.

infobox: Prescription-only in the US, UK, Australia[1]
Both appear on anti-doping prohibited lists[1][2]

paras: Clomiphene was synthesised by Merrell chemists in 1956 and approved in the US in 1967 for inducing ovulation in women. It is on the WHO Essential Medicines List.[1] It is also used off-label in men with low testosterone, and the enclomifene isomer alone is reported to raise testosterone about twice as effectively as the mixture.[1]
Reported adverse effects include visual disturbances, headaches, hot flashes and abdominal discomfort; rarer effects include liver inflammation, raised triglycerides and hair loss.[1]

Enclomifene is the (E)-stereoisomer of clomifene, roughly 62 percent of the clomifene mixture, while the other isomer, zuclomifene, is more estrogenic and can lower testosterone. Enclomifene was investigated for male hypogonadism under the tentative names Androxal and EnCyzix; studies in secondary hypogonadism reported increased total and free testosterone and, in a 2013 comparison with testosterone gel, higher sperm counts. In January 2018 the EMA's CHMP recommended refusing marketing authorization for secondary hypogonadism, and development was discontinued for all indications in April 2021.[3]

hCG is made by placental cells and is used clinically to treat certain forms of hypogonadism, to maintain fertility and testicular size in men on testosterone therapy, and to trigger ovulation.[2] Prolonged use in males can increase androgen production, and caution is advised in people with heart failure, hypertension, kidney dysfunction, migraines or epilepsy.[2] In the 1970s the FDA required a disclaimer on hCG weight-loss advertising, and in 2011 banned over-the-counter hCG diet products.[2]

Proponents in appearance communities reason that raising endogenous testosterone while avoiding testosterone replacement could support a deeper voice. The Wikipedia articles on these drugs list fertility, hypogonadism and testicular function as the uses and do not mention voice effects.[1][2][3] No published trial was identified that measured vocal pitch or resonance in adults after either drug.

Puberphonia is a functional voice disorder in which a high, falsetto-like voice persists after puberty, usually beginning between ages 11 and 15 and most often diagnosed in males. It is usually psychogenic, and treatment is mainly direct voice therapy with a speech-language pathologist lasting one to two weeks, with surgery for therapy-resistant cases; the article notes only that hypogonadism should be ruled out when the thyroid laminae have not fused.[4] On T Nation, one member with a young teenage voice and low testosterone discussed his bloodwork on testosterone therapy.[5]
No studies found on hCG or clomiphene for voice. Studies of enclomifene in secondary hypogonadism are summarized above and examined testosterone and sperm outcomes.[3]
Both drugs require a prescription in the US, UK and Australia, and both appear on anti-doping lists; several athletes have been sanctioned for hCG.[1][2]

card.summary: Two fertility drugs that raise testosterone, floated for voice depth; no voice evidence exists.
card.note: Prescription drugs with their own documented adverse effects; no voice studies.

quick.overview:
hCG and clomiphene are prescription drugs that raise the body's own testosterone, used for fertility and low testosterone. Some online discussion links them to a deeper voice.

No published studies have tested either drug for voice pitch or resonance in adults.
quick.mechanism: hCG mimics luteinizing hormone and stimulates testosterone production in the testes. Clomiphene blocks estrogen feedback in the brain, increasing the signals (GnRH, LH, FSH) that drive testosterone production.
quick.risks: Clomiphene can cause visual disturbances, headaches and hot flashes; hCG carries cautions for several conditions. Both are prescription-only in the US, UK and Australia and are banned in competitive sport.
